drills.q: What is the cited RPS figure for Go (Fiber/Gin-class) vs FastAPI on a JSON CRUD benchmark?
Does making a CPU-bound Python handler async fix its throughput ceiling? Why or why not.
drills.a: No. Async improves I/O concurrency (cooperative waiting), not CPU parallelism -- the GIL still serializes actual bytecode execution regardless of async structure.

drills.q: What migration pattern should a justified Go rewrite follow: big-bang full rewrite, or something else?
drills.a: Strangler-fig: one proven-bottlenecked endpoint or service at a time, shadowed then gradually cut over, never a full-backend big-bang rewrite.

drills.q: A team proposes a Go rewrite citing 'Python is slow' with no profiling data. What's the correct first response, and why?
drills.a: Ask what profiling evidence shows the framework itself, not the database, a blocking call, or missing caching, is the bottleneck. Most 'FastAPI is slow' complaints trace back to those non-framework causes, which are fixable in Python for a fraction of a rewrite's cost -- proposing a rewrite without that evidence risks spending weeks on a guess.

drills.q: A Go rewrite of a 'slow' endpoint shows disappointing improvement over the Python version. What's the most likely explanation?
drills.a: The original bottleneck was never the framework -- likely a slow database query, N+1 queries, or a missing index -- so the same problem exists identically in the Go version against the same schema. The rewrite didn't address the actual cause.

drills.q: Why does a synthetic load-test benchmark showing Go 3.7x faster than FastAPI potentially overstate the real-world production improvement?
drills.a: A synthetic CRUD benchmark isolates pure framework overhead with no real database or downstream calls -- exactly the condition where language choice is the entire cost. Most real production requests are dominated by I/O (database round trips, downstream API latency) that's identical in both languages, so the framework-overhead gap contributes a much smaller fraction of real end-to-end latency.

drills.q: What specific thing breaks for existing API clients if a Go rewrite changes FastAPI's validation error response shape, even if the underlying validation logic is functionally equivalent?
drills.a: Any client parsing the structured error body (FastAPI's {"detail":[{"loc","msg","type"}]} shape) to map errors back to specific form fields breaks silently, since it depends on the exact wire format, not just the logical behavior of rejecting invalid input.

drills.q: Design the decision process for a CPU-bound Python endpoint that's confirmed (via profiling) to be genuinely compute-limited, not I/O-bound. What are the escalating options before a full service rewrite?
drills.a: 1) Algorithmic/implementation optimization of the hot path itself, often overlooked. 2) Horizontal scaling via more uvicorn worker processes, if the per-process memory duplication cost is acceptable, possibly combined with externalizing shared state to Redis to reduce duplication. 3) Offloading just the CPU-bound component to Go/Rust, called from the rest of the Python service. 4) Only if the whole service's profile justifies it, a full service rewrite.

drills.q: A team completes one successful, measured Go migration and leadership wants to rewrite the entire backend on that basis. What's the correct response and why?
drills.a: One measured success validates that specific migration's bottleneck diagnosis, not a blanket 'Go is better, rewrite everything' conclusion. Apply the same profile-first discipline independently to each additional candidate service -- most services proposed next may turn out to be database-bound or cache-missing rather than framework-bound, exactly the pattern cited in real postmortems of rewrites that didn't pay back.

drills.q: Design the shadow-traffic phase of a strangler-fig migration to catch a subtle behavioral divergence before full cutover. What happens when a divergence is found?
drills.a: Route a copy of real production traffic to the new Go service in parallel with the Python service actually serving the response; programmatically diff status codes, response bodies (including error shapes), and latency, logging divergences without ever exposing the shadow response to real users, across enough volume and time to surface rare edge cases. On finding a divergence: a cosmetic difference can be fixed and migration continued; a semantic difference (wrong data, an unfaithfully-ported validation rule) should pause cutover for that path until fixed and re-verified.
